name: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
title: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
answer: Data warehouses and lakehouses store an organisation's analytical history in tables queried with SQL. The major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. This topic covers cloud warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift, and lakehouse formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi. The line between the two has blurred, as warehouses add open table formats and lakehouses add SQL engines. Even this site runs on a PostgreSQL database, which shows how central relational storage remains to analytical work.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on cloud object storage and distributed compute clusters, with columnar file formats and vectorized query engines. Lakehouses typically store data as Parquet or ORC files on object storage, while warehouses manage their own storage and compute layers. AI workloads add GPUs or specialized accelerators for model training and inference, often attached to the same cluster that runs SQL. This site currently tracks 2451 active Model Context Protocol servers, and 263 of them are for SQL databases and warehouses, which shows how many integration points exist between models and analytical storage.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done with SQL for transformation and analysis, plus Python or SQL user-defined functions for model training and inference. Data engineers build pipelines that load raw data into bronze, silver, and gold layers, then analysts and data scientists query those layers. Retrieval augmented generation often uses vector indexes stored alongside relational tables, so a single query can join structured records with embedding search. Model Context Protocol servers let an AI assistant call warehouse tools, run queries, and fetch schema information without custom glue code. The 263 MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses are a practical sign of this pattern.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers access control, data lineage, audit logging, and compliance with regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA. Keeping data inside the warehouse means AI functions inherit the platform's row-level security, masking policies, and encryption, which reduces the risk of data leaking to external services. Provenance matters for both the data and the model, so teams track which tables and versions were used for training or inference. Risks include cost overruns from unmonitored queries, stale features, and vendor lock-in when AI functions are proprietary. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter integration of AI and SQL, with open table formats becoming the default for lakehouses and warehouses alike. Natural language to SQL interfaces and autonomous agents are maturing, and Model Context Protocol is emerging as a common way to connect them to governed data. Research is moving toward in-database machine learning, federated learning across warehouses, and better vector search inside SQL engines. The number of MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses will likely grow as more platforms expose their capabilities. This site's library of 135 research papers and 732 AI tools tracks some of that movement.
